question: What is the primary definition of ambulation in healthcare?

options.B: The ability of a patient to walk
options.C: The safe transfer from bed to chair
options.D: The prevention of blood clots in legs

explanation: Ambulation simply means walking, whether done completely on one's own or with the help of a device or another person. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h1)

question: Why is maintaining a patient's mobility considered vital for overall health?

options.A: It shortens the required hospital stay to one day
options.B: It guarantees complete recovery from any surgery
options.C: It completely eliminates the need for pain medication
options.D: It supports circulation and preserves muscle mass

explanation: Movement keeps blood flowing properly and prevents muscles from weakening quickly during illness or recovery. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h1)

question: Which body systems work together to create coordinated movement?
explanation: Movement requires the structural support of bones and muscles directed and coordinated by the nervous system. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h2)

question: What is the primary role of skeletal muscles during ambulation?

options.A: Contracting to pull bones and create motion
options.B: Sending electrical signals to the brain
options.C: Producing red blood cells for oxygen transport
options.D: Absorbing shock within the joint spaces

explanation: Skeletal muscles shorten and pull on bones across joints to move the body forward during walking. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h2)

question: What is a primary goal of performing a nursing mobility assessment?

options.A: To replace the need for physical therapy input
options.B: To determine functional capacity and plan safe care
options.C: To diagnose underlying genetic bone disorders
options.D: To measure exact daily caloric requirements

explanation: Assessing mobility shows what a patient can safely do on their own and what help they need. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h3)

question: A patient is asked to stand up from a chair, walk ten feet, turn around, and sit back down. What is this clinical observation called?
explanation: The Get-Up-and-Go test is a quick, practical way to evaluate a patient's balance, sit-to-stand transition, and walking stability. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h3)

question: On which side of the body should a patient hold a single-point walking cane?

options.C: The weak side of the body
options.D: The strong side of the body

explanation: Holding the cane on the strong side allows the patient to lean weight onto the device while moving the weaker leg forward. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h4)

question: A patient using axillary crutches complains of numbness and tingling in their fingers. What instruction should the nurse provide?

options.A: Switch immediately to using a standard four-wheeled walker
options.B: Adjust the crutches so they fit higher up in the armpit
options.C: Lean your upper body forward to relieve hand pressure
options.D: Support your body weight on your hands, not your armpits

explanation: Resting body weight on the armpits compresses nerves and blood vessels, leading to nerve damage and tingling; weight must go through the hand grips. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h4)

question: What is the primary safety item a nurse should place around a patient's waist before assisting with a transfer?
explanation: A gait belt gives the nurse a safe, secure handhold to support the patient without pulling on their clothing or arms. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h5)

question: Why is it important for a nurse to keep a wide stance and bend their knees when lifting or moving a patient?

options.A: To increase upper body muscular strength instantly
options.B: To prevent the patient from feeling nervous or unsteady
options.C: To ensure the patient can place their feet flat on the floor
options.D: To lower the center of gravity and protect the back

explanation: Proper body mechanics with a wide base of support reduces strain on the nurse's lumbar spine during physical maneuvers. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h5)

question: How often should a bedbound patient ideally be repositioned to prevent pressure injuries?

options.D: Once per day during the morning shift

explanation: Turning or repositioning a patient every two hours relieves continuous pressure on vulnerable skin areas and tissues. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h6)

question: Which complication is most directly linked to sluggish blood flow in the legs of an immobile patient?
explanation: Immobility slows venous return from the lower extremities, which allows blood clots to form more easily in deep veins. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h6)

question: Which of the following is a common home hazard that frequently leads to patient falls?

options.D: Loose scatter rugs on slick floors

explanation: Loose rugs easily slip underfoot or catch assistive device tips, making them a major tripping hazard in homes. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h7)

question: A patient with unsteady balance prepares for discharge home. What is the best nursing action to address home safety?

options.A: Discuss removing tripping hazards and installing bathroom grab bars
options.B: Advise the patient to remain in bed until fully recovered
options.C: Recommend replacing all furniture with hospital-grade equipment
options.D: Suggest wearing thick socks for warmth and comfort while walking

explanation: Practical modifications like clearing walkways and adding bathroom grab bars directly prevent falls in the living environment. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h7)
